title: Humour and teasing
job: Banter, irony, and when not to
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE REGISTER OF THIS MODULE IS PLAUTINE, NOT MARTIAL, AND THAT IS A DECISION. Latin's two surviving comic voices are far apart: Plautus is broad, affectionate and full of abuse a friend would take; Martial is precise and often cruel. This course writes the Plautine end — teasing a friend, not humiliating a stranger, and nothing that needs a footnote. ō stulte to a friend is affectionate and to a stranger it is an insult, and every usage line in this module says which situation it belongs to.

THE VOCATIVE FINALLY ARRIVES, AND IT ARRIVES AS A JOKE. L2-M7 wanted Mārce for a telephone call and could not have it; L1 got away without one because every name it greeted — Iūlia, magister, discipula — has an address shape identical to its subject shape, and Mārcus does not. Mock address is where a vocative is most audible, so teasing gets it and phoning did not. Mārce is a DIFFERENT SURFACE from L1-M1's Mārcus and a different key. It goes at either end of its sentence, and the END is the commoner position, because an address is more often an afterthought than an opening.

THE CHEAPEST JOKE IN THE LANGUAGE COSTS NOTHING NEW. L2-M9 taught -issimus and said it means 'most' and 'very'; optimē has been in your mouth since L1-M2 as the answer to quid agis?. Said over a broken table it is sarcasm — and the only thing that has changed is the situation, because Latin's words carry no tone of their own. THAT IS WHY IRONY HERE NEEDS THE CONTRADICTION SUPPLIED: optimē legis on its own is praise, and optimē legis: librum nōn habēs is a joke.

nimium AND tandem ARE THE MODULE's TWO TONE WORDS AND NEITHER TAKES AN ENDING. nimium ('too much') is plain exaggeration. tandem carries nothing but impatience — quid tandem agis?, 'what on earth are you doing?' — and English needs a phrase where Latin has a word. Neither changes what is being said; both change how the speaker feels about it, which is the whole apparatus of teasing and costs two indeclinable words.

quid agis? WAS 'HOW ARE YOU?' IN THE SECOND MODULE OF THIS COURSE AND HERE IT IS A DEMAND. tandem is what changes it, and the pair is worth noticing because it shows how little of tone lives in vocabulary: the same three words are a greeting and an accusation depending on one particle. rīdēs, sed nōn rīdeō is the same point — one verb twice, no pronouns, and a whole disagreement in the endings.

enim COMES SECOND IN ITS CLAUSE, NOT IN THE SENTENCE, and that distinction is the thing about these six words that takes longest to believe. Nimium enim bibistī has enim after the first word of ITS clause, which begins deep inside the sentence. The six are autem, enim, igitur, quoque, vērō and tamen, and L1-M10 settled the rule forty rungs ago.

A FUTURE CAN BE A THREAT, AND NOTHING BUT THE CONTRAST MAKES IT ONE. L1-M6 taught the -bis future forty-four modules ago as a plain statement about later; sed nōn rīdēbis after rīdēs is a warning. This is as close as this module comes to Martial and it stops there deliberately — a threat in play is Plautine, and a threat meant is not what this course teaches.

sentences.cue: Oh Marcus, you read too much.

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.

'Too much, too'. It takes no ending and it sits before what it exaggerates — plain overstatement, with no irony in the word itself.
'You read' — legō, legis, legit, legimus. L1-M4's verb.

words.note: 'Very well, excellently'. L1-M2's word — and said of an obvious disaster it means the opposite, exactly as English 'brilliant' does. The word has not changed; the situation has.
'Table' as the subject. L1-M3's word.
'Broken' — L2-M8's participle used as an adjective, agreeing with mēnsa.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum, es, est, sunt.

mistake.why: the adjective where the adverb belongs. optimus describes a person or thing and optimē describes how something is done — and L1-M2 taught the adverb, which is the form that carries the sarcasm.

sentences.mnemonic: The word is L1-M2's; only the situation is new.

sentences.cue: Oh you fool, what on earth are you doing?

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Fool!' — the vocative of stultus, 'foolish'. Between friends it is affectionate; to a stranger it is not, which is the module's whole register question.
'What', asking. L1-M2's word.
'Really, pray, on earth'. It carries impatience and nothing else, and English needs a phrase ('on earth') where Latin has a word.
'You do' — L1-M2's agō. quid agis? was 'how are you?'; with tandem in it, it is a real and impatient question.

sentences.trap: quid agis? was 'how are you?' in the second module of this course and here it is a demand. tandem is what changes it — a word that carries nothing but impatience, where English needs a phrase ('on earth', 'in heaven's name') — and between friends ō stulte is affectionate. To a stranger it is not.
sentences.sound: Ō STUL-te, QUID TAN-dem A-gis? Eight syllables and one long vowel, which is the ō.

variations.cue: What on earth are you doing?
variations.changed: no address, which is impatient without being rude

variations.cue: Oh you fool, how are you?
variations.changed: tandem dropped, which turns it back into L1-M2's greeting and makes the insult the joke

variations.cue: Oh Marcus, what on earth are you doing?
variations.changed: a name instead of an insult

mistake.why: the subject shape used as an insult. stulte is how you call somebody a fool and stultus is how you describe one — the same error as S01's plate on a different word, which is what happens when a case arrives at the fiftieth module.

sentences.usage: Said to a friend who is being ridiculous. Not to a stranger.
sentences.mnemonic: tandem is a word for what English needs a phrase for.

sentences.cue: You are laughing, but I am not.

words.note: 'You laugh': rīdeō 'I laugh', rīdēs 'you laugh', rīdet 'he laughs'. English 'ridiculous' and 'deride' come from it.
'But'. L1-M9's word, joining two clauses from the front.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I laugh' — the same verb, first person. The sentence is one verb twice and the contrast is entirely in the endings.

sentences.trap: One verb twice and a whole disagreement. The joke has landed for one person and not the other, and Latin says it in four words with no pronouns at all — because the endings carry who, which is what forty rungs of pro-drop have been for.
sentences.sound: RĪ-dēs, SED nōn RĪ-de-ō. Seven syllables, and the two long ī sounds are the same verb twice.

variations.cue: You are laughing, but I am NOT.
variations.changed: ego added, which makes the contrast pointed

variations.cue: He is laughing, but I am not.
variations.changed: someone else laughing

variations.cue: You are laughing; I am laughing too.
variations.changed: L1-M10's quoque, second in its clause, and the joke shared

mistake.why: the same ending twice, which says 'you are laughing but you are not laughing'. The whole sentence is one verb in two persons, so getting the second ending wrong makes it a contradiction rather than a disagreement.

sentences.usage: Said when a joke has gone wrong.
sentences.mnemonic: The endings carry who; no pronouns needed.

sentences.cue: You have drunk too much, you fool.

words.note: 'Too much, too'. It takes no ending and it sits before what it exaggerates — plain overstatement, with no irony in the word itself.
'You drank' — the perfect's you-shape of bibō, -istī where the present is -is. L4-M10's vēnistī was the same ending.
'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Fool!' — the vocative of stultus, 'foolish'. Between friends it is affectionate; to a stranger it is not, which is the module's whole register question.

sentences.trap: A vocative at the END of its sentence, which is where Latin usually puts it. L2-M7 could not write one at all; this module shows it both at the front (S01, S03) and at the back — and the back is the commoner position, because an address is an afterthought more often than an opening.
sentences.sound: NI-mi-um bi-BIS-tī, Ō STUL-te. Nine syllables and three long vowels, two of them in the insult.

variations.cue: You have drunk too much.
variations.changed: the insult dropped, which is a rebuke rather than teasing

variations.cue: Oh you fool, you have drunk too much.
variations.changed: the vocative at the front, which is heavier

variations.cue: I have drunk too much.
variations.changed: about the speaker, which is an admission and not a joke

mistake.why: the subject shape again, this time at the end of the sentence where the ear is least careful. Three plates in five sentences on one case — which is what a shape deferred for forty-nine modules costs when it finally lands.

sentences.usage: Said to a friend the next morning.
sentences.mnemonic: A vocative goes at either end, and the end is commoner.

sentences.display: Optimē legis, ō stulte: librum nōn habēs.
sentences.cue: You read beautifully, you fool: you do not have a book.
sentences.literal: excellently you-read O fool! book not you-have

words.note: 'Very well' — L1-M2's word, and sarcastic here because what follows contradicts it.
'You read' — legō, legis, legit.
'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Fool!' — the vocative of stultus, 'foolish'. Between friends it is affectionate; to a stranger it is not, which is the module's whole register question.
'Book' as the object. L1-M4's word.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'You have' — habeō, habēs, habet. L1-M1's verb.

sentences.trap: The sarcasm and the reason for it, in one sentence. optimē legis is praise; librum nōn habēs is why it is not — and the colon does the work English does with a dash. Latin's irony needs the contradiction supplied, because the words carry no tone of their own.
sentences.sound: op-ti-MĒ LE-gis, Ō STUL-te: LI-brum nōn HA-bēs. Fourteen syllables and four long vowels.

variations.cue: You read beautifully: you do not have a book.

variations.display: Optimē legis, ō Mārce: librum nōn habēs.

variations.changed: the sarcasm dropped entirely

mistake.display: Optimē legis, ō stulte: librum nōn habeō.
mistake.why: the wrong person on the second verb, which turns the joke on the speaker: 'you read beautifully — I don't have a book'. The sarcasm needs the contradiction to be about the person being teased.

sentences.cue: What on earth are you saying? You are laughing too much.

words.note: 'What', asking. L1-M2's word.
'Really, pray, on earth'. It carries impatience and nothing else, and English needs a phrase ('on earth') where Latin has a word.
'You say' — dīcō, dīcis, dīcit, dīxit. L3-M5's verb.
'Too much, too'. It takes no ending and it sits before what it exaggerates — plain overstatement, with no irony in the word itself.
'You laugh' — rīdeō, rīdēs, rīdet.

sentences.trap: tandem in a question and nimium in a statement, and both are doing tone rather than meaning. Neither changes what is being said; both change how the speaker feels about it — which is the whole apparatus of teasing in this language and costs two indeclinable words.
sentences.sound: QUID TAN-dem DĪ-cis? NI-mi-um RĪ-dēs. Ten syllables and three long vowels.

variations.changed: L1-M2's agis instead

mistake.why: an adjective where the indeclinable belongs. nimium never changes — it is not describing anybody — and nimius would be trying to agree with a subject that is already inside the verb.

sentences.usage: Said to somebody who will not stop laughing.
sentences.mnemonic: Neither tone word takes an ending.

sentences.display: Ō Mārce, optimē! Nimium enim bibistī.
sentences.cue: Oh Marcus, brilliant! For you have drunk too much.
sentences.literal: O Marcus! excellently too-much for you-drank

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Marcus!' as ADDRESS — the vocative, and a different shape from L1-M1's Mārcus. This course wanted it at L2-M7 for a telephone call and had to wait until here.
'Very well' — L1-M2's word, sarcastic because of what follows.
'Too much, too'. It takes no ending and it sits before what it exaggerates — plain overstatement, with no irony in the word itself.
'For' — and it comes SECOND in its clause, never first. L1-M10's word, and one of six that must.
'You drank' — bibō's perfect in the you-shape.

sentences.trap: enim second, in a clause whose first word is nimium. The position rule is about the CLAUSE and not about the sentence, so enim lands after the first word of its own clause however deep in the sentence that clause begins — which is the thing about these six words that takes longest to believe.
sentences.sound: Ō MĀR-ce, op-ti-MĒ! NI-mi-um E-nim bi-BIS-tī. Thirteen syllables and four long vowels.

variations.cue: Oh Marcus, brilliant! You have drunk too much.
variations.changed: enim dropped, which loses the 'for'

variations.cue: Brilliant! For you have drunk too much.
variations.changed: the address dropped

variations.cue: Oh Marcus, you have drunk too much.
variations.changed: the sarcasm dropped, which is a straight rebuke

mistake.display: Ō Mārce, optimē! Enim nimium bibistī.
mistake.why: enim first, which cannot happen. It must come second in its clause — L1-M10 settled that forty rungs ago — and English's 'for' at the head of a clause is what makes this the commonest misplacement of the six.

sentences.usage: Said to a friend, with an edge.
sentences.mnemonic: enim is second in its CLAUSE, not in the sentence.

sentences.display: Rīdēs, ō stulte; sed nōn rīdēbis.
sentences.cue: You are laughing, you fool; but you will not be laughing.
sentences.literal: you-laugh O fool! but not you-will-laugh

words.note: 'You laugh' — rīdeō, rīdēs, rīdet.
'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Fool!' — the vocative of stultus, 'foolish'. Between friends it is affectionate; to a stranger it is not, which is the module's whole register question.
'But'. L1-M9's word.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'You will laugh' — L1-M6's -bis future on rīdeō, like labōrābis. The threat is entirely in the tense.

sentences.trap: The whole threat is a tense. L1-M6 taught the future forty-four modules ago as a plain statement about later; here the same ending is a warning, and nothing but the contrast with the present makes it one. This is as close as this module comes to Martial and it stops there.
sentences.sound: RĪ-dēs, Ō STUL-te; SED nōn rī-DĒ-bis. Eleven syllables and five long vowels.

variations.cue: You are laughing; but you will not be laughing.
variations.changed: the insult dropped, which is colder

variations.display: Rīdēs, ō stulte; sed crās nōn rīdēbis.
variations.cue: You are laughing, you fool; but tomorrow you will not be.
variations.changed: L1-M4's crās, which makes the threat specific

variations.cue: You will laugh.
variations.changed: the future alone, which is a promise rather than a threat

mistake.display: Rīdēs, ō stulte; sed nōn rīdēs.
mistake.why: the present where the future belongs, which removes the threat and leaves a contradiction. The whole menace of the sentence is one ending, and it is L1-M6's.

sentences.usage: Said as a warning, in play.
sentences.mnemonic: A future can be a threat.

sentences.display: Ō stulte, quid tandem agis? Optimē! Nimium enim bibistī, et nōn iam rīdēbis.
sentences.cue: Oh you fool, what on earth are you doing? Brilliant! For you have drunk too much, and you will not be laughing any more.
sentences.literal: O fool! what really you-do excellently too-much for you-drank and not already you-will-laugh

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address, and it makes a vocative louder. It is optional before a name and obligatory before an insult.
'Fool!' — the vocative of stultus, 'foolish'. Between friends it is affectionate; to a stranger it is not, which is the module's whole register question.
'What', asking. L1-M2's word.
'Really, pray, on earth'. It carries impatience and nothing else, and English needs a phrase ('on earth') where Latin has a word.
'You do' — L1-M2's agō, and quid agis? was that module's greeting.
'Very well' — L1-M2's word, sarcastic.
'Too much, too'. It takes no ending and it sits before what it exaggerates — plain overstatement, with no irony in the word itself.
'For' — second in its clause, never first.
'You drank' — bibō's perfect in the you-shape.
'And'. L1-M1's word.
'Not' — and nōn iam together mean 'no longer'. L4-M6's pair.
'Already' — and with nōn in front, 'no longer'. L4-M6's word.
'You will laugh' — L1-M6's future of rīdeō.

sentences.trap: Every tone device in the module at once: a vocative insult, an impatient question word, a sarcastic adverb, an exaggeration, a second-position connective and a threatening future. Not one of them is a new grammatical system — the vocative is the module's only new shape — and the whole thing is built out of L1 and L2 with two indeclinable words on top.
sentences.sound: Twenty-three syllables in four clauses. Read it as four, and each one carries one device.

mistake.display: Ō stultus, quid tandem agis? Optimus! Enim nimium bibistī.
mistake.why: three errors at once, one per device: the subject shape as an insult, the adjective where the sarcastic adverb belongs, and enim at the head of its clause. It is what this sentence looks like when a learner has all six devices and none of the shapes.

sentences.usage: Said to a close friend and to nobody else.
sentences.mnemonic: One new shape, six devices, forty-nine rungs of ladder.
